Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation

$$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$

and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map

$$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$

assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore

$$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$

which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$.

**Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

**Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$,
and for $x,y\in H$ define

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad E_{x,y}(B):=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle \qquad(B\in\Sigma).$$

Then:

1. $E_x$ is a positive measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ with $E_x(X)=\|x\|^2$ and
   $0\le E_x(B)\le\|x\|^2$ for every $B$;
2. $E_{x,y}$ is a finite complex measure on $(X,\Sigma)$, the map
   $(x,y)\mapsto E_{x,y}$ is linear in $x$ and conjugate-linear in $y$, and
   $E_{y,x}=\overline{E_{x,y}}$, meaning $E_{y,x}(B)=\overline{E_{x,y}(B)}$ for
   every $B$;
3. $|E_{x,y}|(X)\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so $|E_{x,y}(B)|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$ for every
   $B$, and the polarization identity
   $$E_{x,y}=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3}i^kE_{x+i^ky}$$
   holds as an identity of complex measures, where $i^k$ are the fourth roots
   of unity $1,i,-1,-i$.

Let $\mathcal A_0$ be an algebra of subsets of $X$. A **premeasure** on an algebra $\mathcal A_0$ vanishes at the empty set and is countably additive whenever a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal A_0$ has its union in $\mathcal A_0$. Thus $\mu_0:\mathcal A_0\to[0,+\infty]$ is a premeasure when $\mu_0(\varnothing)=0$ and

$$\mu_0\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}A_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu_0(A_k)$$

whenever the $A_k$ are pairwise disjoint members of $\mathcal A_0$ and their union belongs to $\mathcal A_0$. Padding a finite disjoint family by empty sets shows that a premeasure is finitely additive.

The premeasure is **finite** if $\mu_0(X)<+\infty$. It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal A_0$ with $X=\bigcup_nP_n$ and $\mu_0(P_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The outer set function induced by a premeasure is an outer measure.
For an outer measure $\mu^*$ on $X$, the Carathéodory measurable subsets form a sigma-algebra, and the restriction of the outer measure to it is a complete measure.
For every $A\in\mathcal A_0$, the outer measure induced by a premeasure satisfies $\mu^*(A)=\mu_0(A)$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every member of the source algebra is Carathéodory measurable for the induced outer measure.
A finite premeasure has at most one measure extension to the sigma-algebra generated by its source algebra.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **pi-system on $X$** is a nonempty family
$\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ closed under binary intersections: if
$A,B\in\mathcal P$, then $A\cap B\in\mathcal P$.

The nonempty-family requirement is the convention used here. It does not require
$X\in\mathcal P$ and it does not add an empty-intersection axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $X$ be LCH and suppose every open subset of $X$ is sigma-compact. Every Borel measure finite on compact sets is regular: it is outer regular on Borel sets and inner regular by compact sets on every Borel set.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

derivations.claim: [The finitely additive projection on the rectangle algebra] For a finite disjoint union $A=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^n(B_i\times C_i)$ of measurable rectangles put $P(A):=\sum_iE(B_i)F(C_i)$. This is well defined: two finite rectangle decompositions have a common refinement into disjoint rectangles (intersections of the pieces), and on a common refinement both sums agree by additivity of $E$ and $F$; in particular $P(\varnothing)=0$ and $P(\mathbb R^2)=I$. Each $E(B_i)F(C_i)$ is an orthogonal projection because $(E(B_i)F(C_i))^2=E(B_i)^2F(C_i)^2=E(B_i)F(C_i)$ and $(E(B_i)F(C_i))^*=F(C_i)E(B_i)=E(B_i)F(C_i)$ by [F1] and strong commutation; summands belonging to disjoint rectangles are orthogonal, since $E(B_i)F(C_i)E(B_j)F(C_j)=E(B_i\cap B_j)F(C_i\cap C_j)=0$. Hence $P(A)$ is a sum of pairwise orthogonal projections, so $P(A)^2=P(A)=P(A)^*$; and from the refinement description $P$ is finitely additive on disjoint unions, $P(A\cap A')=P(A)P(A')$ and $P(A\cup A')=P(A)+P(A')$ for disjoint $A,A'\in\mathcal A_0$.

[Uniqueness for finite complex measures] Let $\mu,
u$ be finite complex measures on $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$ that agree on $\mathcal A_0$, which contains $\mathbb R^2$. Then $\mathcal D:=\{S\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2):\mu(S)=
u(S)\}$ contains $\mathbb R^2$ and the $\pi$-system $\mathcal A_0$; it is a $\lambda$-system because equality on the whole space gives closure under complements and countable additivity gives closure under disjoint countable unions. By Dynkin's $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem [F8], $\mathcal D$ contains $\sigma(\mathcal A_0)=\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$ by [F5], so $\mu=
u$ on every Borel set.

[The scalar set functions are premeasures] For $\psi\in H$ define $\mu_\psi(A):=\langle P(A)\psi,\psi\rangle=\|P(A)\psi\|^2$ for $A\in\mathcal A_0$; by step 1.1, $\mu_\psi(\varnothing)=0$, $\mu_\psi$ is finitely additive, and $\mu_\psi\le\|\psi\|^2$. To verify countable additivity, fix pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal A_0$ with union $A\in\mathcal A_0$ and put $R_N:=A\setminus\bigcup_{n\le N}A_n\in\mathcal A_0$. Finite additivity gives $\mu_\psi(A)=\sum_{n\le N}\mu_\psi(A_n)+\mu_\psi(R_N)$, and $R_N\downarrow\varnothing$, so continuity from above at $\varnothing$ implies $\mu_\psi(A)=\sum_n\mu_\psi(A_n)$. It remains to prove that continuity: for $A_n\downarrow\varnothing$ in $\mathcal A_0$, show $\mu_\psi(A_n)\to0$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, approximate each $A_n$ from inside by a compact union of rectangles: for a rectangle $B\times C$ one has $P(B\times C)-P(K_B\times K_C)=E(B\setminus K_B)F(C)+E(K_B)F(C\setminus K_C)$ with the two summands orthogonal, so $\mu_\psi(B\times C)-\mu_\psi(K_B\times K_C)\le E_\psi(B\setminus K_B)+F_\psi(C\setminus K_C)$ for $E_\psi(B)=\langle E(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$, $F_\psi(C)=\langle F(C)\psi,\psi\rangle$; by regularity [F1] compact $K_B\subseteq B$, $K_C\subseteq C$ make this arbitrarily small, and finite unions are handled by summing. Choose compact $L_n\subseteq A_n$ with $\mu_\psi(A_n\setminus L_n)<\varepsilon2^{-n}$. If $\mu_\psi(A_n)\ge\varepsilon$ for all $n$, then for every $N$ additivity and $L_1\cap\dots\cap L_N\supseteq A_N\setminus\bigcup_{n\le N}(A_n\setminus L_n)$ give $\mu_\psi(L_1\cap\dots\cap L_N)\ge\mu_\psi(A_N)-\sum_{n\le N}\mu_\psi(A_n\setminus L_n)\ge\varepsilon-\sum_{n\le N}\varepsilon2^{-n}>0$; hence every finite intersection $L_1\cap\dots\cap L_N$ is nonempty, and compactness gives a point of $\bigcap_nL_n\subseteq\bigcap_nA_n=\varnothing$, a contradiction. Thus $\mu_\psi(A_n)\to0$, and $\mu_\psi$ is a finite premeasure on $\mathcal A_0$.

[Carathéodory extension and polarization] By steps 1.1 and 2.1 the algebra $\mathcal A_0$ of finite unions of measurable rectangles is a $\pi$-system containing $\mathbb R^2$ and generates $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$ by [F5]; hence $\mu_\psi$ extends to a finite measure $
u_\psi$ on $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$, unique by [F3], and $
u_\psi(S)=\mu_\psi(S)$ for $S\in\mathcal A_0$. Uniqueness also extends the scalar homogeneity $
u_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2
u_x$ and the parallelogram identity from $\mathcal A_0$ to every Borel set: the corresponding finite positive measures agree on $\mathcal A_0$ and have the same total mass. For $x,y\in H$ define $
u_{x,y}(S):= rac14\sum_{k=0}^3i^k
u_{x+i^ky}(S)$; this is a finite complex measure and for $S\in\mathcal A_0$ it coincides with $\langle P(S)x,yangle$ by the polarization identity [F2]. The scalar homogeneity and parallelogram identity imply, by expansion of the four polarization terms, that $(x,y)\mapsto
u_{x,y}(S)$ is sesquilinear and Hermitian for every Borel $S$, with $
u_{x,x}(S)=
u_x(S)\ge0$. Positivity gives Cauchy–Schwarz for this form (apply $0\le
u_{x+\lambda y}(S)$ for all $\lambda\in\mathbb C$), so $|
u_{x,y}(S)|\le
u_x(S)^{1/2}
u_y(S)^{1/2}\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$.

u_{x,y}(S'\cap R)$ and $S'\mapsto\langle G(S')G(R)x,yangle=
u_{G(R)x,y}(S')$ are finite complex measures; they agree on rectangles $S'=B	imes C$ because $G(S'\cap R)=E(B\cap B')F(C\cap C')=E(B)E(B')F(C)F(C')=E(B)F(C)E(B')F(C')=G(S')G(R)$ by [F1] and the commutation hypothesis, and they agree on $\mathbb R^2$ since each value is $G(R)$. By step 1.2 [F8], these scalar measures agree on all Borel $S'$, so $G(S'\cap R)=G(S')G(R)$ for all Borel $S'$. u_{x,G(S)y}(T)$; by the previous result they agree on every rectangle $T$, and by step 1.2 [F8] they agree for all Borel $T$. Taking $S=T$ yields $G(S)^2=G(S)$, so every $G(S)$ is an orthogonal projection; $G(\varnothing)=0$ and $G(\mathbb R^2)=I$ follow from the rectangle values. Strong countable additivity holds because for pairwise disjoint $S_n$ with union $S$ the scalar measures satisfy $
u_x(S)=\sum_n
u_x(S_n)$, so $\sum_n\|G(S_n)x\|^2=\sum_n
u_{x}(S_n)=
u_x(S)\le\|x\|^2<\infty$ and the orthogonal series $\sum_nG(S_n)x$ converges in norm to a vector whose pairings with every $y$ equal $\sum_n
u_{x,y}(S_n)=
u_{x,y}(S)=\langle G(S)x,yangle$, hence to $G(S)x$. Finally the scalar measures of $G$ are the $

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A finite-valued function $f=u+iv:X\to\mathbb C$ is **measurable** when $u,v$ are real measurable functions. Write
$$N_p(f)=\begin{cases}\left(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty,\end{cases}\quad(1\le p<\infty),\qquad N_\infty(f)=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty]:|f|\le M\text{ a.e.}\}.$$
The finite case uses the real power; the infinite case is assigned directly,
so $N_p(f)$ is defined for every measurable finite-valued complex $f$.
The infimum of the empty set of finite bounds is $\infty$; equivalently allow $M=\infty$. Define $\mathcal L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\{f:f\text{ measurable},N_p(f)<\infty\}$ and its **set quotient** $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\mathcal L^p/\!\sim$, where $f\sim g$ means $f=g$ a.e. This extends [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]. Norm and vector-space assertions are established separately.

Here $|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$ and $\overline{u+iv}=u-iv$ as in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. These operations preserve measurability: $u^2+v^2$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and
$$\{|f|>a\}=\begin{cases}\{u^2+v^2>a^2\},&a\ge0,\\X,&a<0.\end{cases}$$
Thus [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]] applies. For $g=a+ib$, the formulas $fg=(ua-vb)+i(ub+va)$ and $\overline f=u-iv$ prove the remaining claims by real arithmetic closure. Nonnegative powers are measurable because $\{r^t>b\}=\{r>b^{1/t}\}$ for $r\ge0,t>0,b\ge0$, with the negative thresholds automatic.

A **finite simple** complex function has finite range and measurable fibers. Its **finite-measure support** condition is $\mu(\{s\ne0\})<\infty$. This concerns the nonzero set, not compactness of its closure. The zero function is an admissible finite simple function, including when $X=\varnothing$ or $\mu(X)=0$.

Integration is componentwise: for integrable $f=u+iv$,
$$\int f\,d\mu=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$
This is the earlier convention of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The inequalities $|u|,|v|\le|f|\le|u|+|v|$ show that integrability of the modulus and integrability of both components are equivalent.

For $n\ge1$, define complex $C_c(\mathbb R^n)$, $C_0(\mathbb R^n)$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ by requiring both components to lie in the corresponding real spaces ([[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]], [[def-c-zero-on-rn]]). Derivatives are componentwise, with the multi-index and all-ordered-partials conventions of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. The union of the two compact component supports is compact. A measurable complex $f$ is **locally integrable** for Lebesgue measure if $\int_K|f|<\infty$ on every compact $K$. The component inequalities give the equivalent componentwise condition. By [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], closed bounded balls are compact and each compact set is bounded. Hence compact integrability implies integrability on every bounded open ball by restriction from its closure; conversely each compact set is contained in a bounded open ball. These prove both directions of the ball formulation.

For a topological $X$ with Borel sets contained in $\mathcal A$, define
$$\operatorname{ess\,supp}_\mu f=X\setminus\bigcup\{U:U\text{ open and }f=0\text{ a.e. on }U\}.$$
Changing $f$ on one measurable null set preserves the zero-a.e. property on every $U$, since the union of that set and the old exceptional set is null. Thus essential support depends only on the a.e. class. Ordinary support means $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}$ and can change with the representative.

For the following illustration assume [[def-countable-choice]]. For $f=\mathbf1_{\mathbb Q}$ on $\mathbb R$, [[prop-countable-subsets-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]] gives $f=0$ Lebesgue-a.e.; therefore $N_\infty(f)=0$ and $\operatorname{ess\,supp}f=\varnothing$, since $U=\mathbb R$ occurs in the union. But [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]] gives $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}=\mathbb R$. For the Dirac probability measure at zero ([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), the bound $1$ holds everywhere and every $0\le M<1$ fails on $\{0\}$, of measure one. Thus $N_{\infty,\delta_0}(f)=1$.

The raw $L^2$ pairing convention is $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$, linear in the first variable. Its integrability and class invariance are obligations of the later pairing items. **Bilinear tests** instead use $\int fs$, with no conjugation of $s$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}=0$ when two of $i,j,k$ coincide, and otherwise $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$; the sum ranges over $k\in\{x,y,z\}$. The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

Let $s,t\in\frac12\mathbb N$, write $L_s:=\{-s,-s+1,\dots,s\}$ and $L_t:=\{-t,-t+1,\dots,t\}$, and let
$(V_s,J^{(s)}_x,J^{(s)}_y,J^{(s)}_z)$ and $(V_t,J^{(t)}_x,J^{(t)}_y,J^{(t)}_z)$ be the spin models of
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]] with orthonormal bases $(e^{(s)}_m)_{m\in L_s}$ and
$(e^{(t)}_n)_{n\in L_t}$ and the ladders $J^{(s)}_\pm:=J^{(s)}_x\pm iJ^{(s)}_y$,
$J^{(t)}_\pm:=J^{(t)}_x\pm iJ^{(t)}_y$ and Casimirs $J^{(s)2}$, $J^{(t)2}$
([[thm-tensor-product-basis-from-bases]]). On the tensor product $V_s\otimes V_t$ put

$$J^{\mathrm{tot}}_i:=J^{(s)}_i\otimes I_{V_t}+I_{V_s}\otimes J^{(t)}_i\quad(i=x,y,z),\qquad J^{\mathrm{tot}}_\pm:=J^{\mathrm{tot}}_x\pm iJ^{\mathrm{tot}}_y,\qquad J^{\mathrm{tot}\,2}:=(J^{\mathrm{tot}}_x)^2+(J^{\mathrm{tot}}_y)^2+(J^{\mathrm{tot}}_z)^2 .$$

Then:

(a) each $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_i$ is self-adjoint, the triple $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_x,J^{\mathrm{tot}}_y,J^{\mathrm{tot}}_z$
satisfies the commutation relations of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-block-decomposition]], and
$J^{\mathrm{tot}\,2}=J^{(s)2}\otimes I_{V_t}+I_{V_s}\otimes J^{(t)2}+2\sum_{i}J^{(s)}_i\otimes J^{(t)}_i$ is
self-adjoint and commutes with $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_x,J^{\mathrm{tot}}_y,J^{\mathrm{tot}}_z$;

(b) there is an orthogonal decomposition $V_s\otimes V_t=\bigoplus_{j=|s-t|}^{s+t}W_j$ into
$J^{\mathrm{tot}}$-invariant subspaces, one for each $j\in\{|s-t|,|s-t|+1,\dots,s+t\}$, with
$\dim W_j=2j+1$, on each of which $(J^{\mathrm{tot}}_x,J^{\mathrm{tot}}_y,J^{\mathrm{tot}}_z)$ is unitarily
equivalent to the spin-$j$ model of [[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]]; consequently
$\sum_{j=|s-t|}^{s+t}(2j+1)=(2s+1)(2t+1)$;

(c) for every $M\in\frac12\mathbb Z$ the $M$-eigenspace of $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_z$ has dimension
$$N(M):=\#\{m\in L_s:\ M-m\in L_t\}=\begin{cases}\max\bigl(0,\ \min(s,M+t)-\max(-s,M-t)+1\bigr),&M-(s+t)\in\mathbb Z,\\0,&M-(s+t)\notin\mathbb Z.\end{cases},$$
and the identity $(e^{(s)}_m\otimes e^{(t)}_n)_{m,n}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V_s\otimes V_t$ consisting of
eigenvectors of $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_z$ with eigenvalues $m+n$;

(d) the number of summands with parameter equal to $M$ in the decomposition of (b) is
$N(M)-N(M+1)$ if $M\ge0$, and this number equals $1$ when $M-(s+t)\in\mathbb Z$ and $|s-t|\le M\le s+t$, and equals $0$ otherwise; hence the
multiset of parameters in (b) is exactly $\{|s-t|,|s-t|+1,\dots,s+t\}$, each occurring once;

(e) for each $j\in\{|s-t|,\dots,s+t\}$ the space of vectors of $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_z$-eigenvalue $j$ orthogonal to
all summands $W_{j'}$ with $j'>j$ is one-dimensional; for a unit vector $u_j$ in it the vectors
$$v_{j,k}:=\bigl(k!(2j)(2j-1)\cdots(2j-k+1)\bigr)^{-1/2}(J^{\mathrm{tot}}_-)^ku_j\qquad(0\le k\le2j)$$
form an orthonormal basis of $W_j$ with $J^{\mathrm{tot}}_zv_{j,k}=(j-k)v_{j,k}$,
$J^{\mathrm{tot}}_+v_{j,k}=\sqrt{k(2j-k+1)}\,v_{j,k-1}$ and
$J^{\mathrm{tot}}_-v_{j,k}=\sqrt{(k+1)(2j-k)}\,v_{j,k+1}$; the coefficients of $v_{j,k}$ in the product basis
are therefore determined by the phase of $u_j$, and choosing that phase fixes the Clebsch-Gordan numbers
explicitly; in particular $u_{s+t}=e^{(s)}_s\otimes e^{(t)}_t$ is a permissible choice.

The theorem is a purely mathematical statement about tensor products of the explicit matrices of
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]]; it asserts no physical coupling, conservation law or
measurement fact.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following assignments for identical species and for spin. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

**(i) Labels and sectors.** For $n$ particles of one species the model forms the $n$-fold completed tensor power $H^{\otimes n}$ of the one-particle space ([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]), whose tensor position factors are mathematical labels and not observable particle identities. For a declared **bosonic species** the model uses the symmetric sector $S^{n}H$, the range of the symmetrizing projection $P_{n}^{+}$, and for a declared **fermionic species** the antisymmetric sector $\Lambda^{n}H$, the range of the alternating projection, both as constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. The sector is part of the declared species assignment; the permutation invariance of states in the sector and the resulting exclusion statement for fermions are conditional consequences read off that projection, not assumptions added to it. A bounded quantity $A$ on $H^{\otimes n}$ is restricted to an adopted sector only when it preserves that sector; in particular, $AU_\pi=U_\pi A$ for every permutation implies $AP_n^{\pm}=P_n^{\pm}A$ by the finite projection sums. Bounded tensor maps construct ambient operators; an operator on a single labelled factor need not preserve either sector.

**(ii) Spin.** For a declared **spin label** $s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$ the model assigns the internal factor $V_s=\mathbb C^{2s+1}$ with the standard inner product and basis $(e_m)_{m=-s,-s+1,\ldots,s}$. Here $SU(2)=\{W\in M_2(\mathbb C):W^*W=I_2,\det W=1\}$ with its matrix topology. For $s>0$ put $n=2s\ge1$ and let $F_s:\mathcal S_n\to V_s$ be the unitary identification $F_sv_k=e_{s-k}$ of [[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-symmetric-power-su2-representation]]. The assigned strongly continuous unitary representation is $D_s(W)=F_sU_n(W)F_s^{-1}$. For $s=0$ put $D_0(W)=I_{\mathbb C}$ for every $W$, the trivial one-dimensional representation with zero generators. The spin operators are $S_i=\hbar J_i$ with the self-adjoint endomorphisms of [[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]], satisfying
$$[S_i,S_j]=i\hbar\sum_k\epsilon_{ijk}S_k,\qquad S^2=S_x^2+S_y^2+S_z^2=\hbar^2s(s+1)I.$$
For $A_i(t)=\cos(t/2)I_2-i\sin(t/2)\sigma_i$, the curve $D_s(A_i(t))$ has infinitesimal generator $-iJ_i$, including $s=0$. This specifies the internal $SU(2)$ action. If a spatial Hilbert factor $H_{\mathrm{sp}}$ is separately assigned a strongly continuous unitary $SU(2)$ representation $R_{\mathrm{sp}}$, the combined action is explicitly $W\mapsto R_{\mathrm{sp}}(W)\otimes D_s(W)$ on $H_{\mathrm{sp}}\widehat\otimes V_s$: its representation law follows from bounded tensor composition, and continuity follows on elementary tensors and then by density and the unitary norm bound. The existence and physical interpretation of that spatial action require the separate assignment. The spin label and representation are species model assignments; the internal factor is not a rotating body or a spatial coordinate.

**(iii) Species parameters.** The mass, charge, spin label, statistics and any magnetic coupling constant of a species are empirical model parameters: they enter the model as declared values with uncertainty, and no value is derived from the Hilbert-space formalism. The assignment of a sector (symmetric or antisymmetric) to a species is likewise a model assignment, tested through the consequences computed with it.

**(iv) What is not asserted.** The relativistic spin-statistics theorem is not a theorem of this postulate set: the connection between spin and permutation sector adopted here is a nonrelativistic model assignment, and any relativistic statement about it belongs to a framework that adopts relativistic assumptions. Similarly, the postulate asserts nothing about the internal structure, compositeness or interactions of a species beyond the declared parameters.

**(v) Status.** Clauses (i)-(iv) are adopted assumptions of the framework for declared species. They record the sectors and the spin representations used by the model and the empirical status of the species parameters; they make no claim that the model assignment is exact for any species and record no measurement.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework, for systems in the declared massive-matter sector, the following statements about states and their composition. Assume throughout the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the mathematical suppliers cited below.

**(i) State space.** To each physical system of the sector the model assigns a complex Hilbert space $H$ that is nonzero and separable: a complex Hilbert space in the sense of [[def-hilbert-space]] which admits a sequence whose range is dense in $H$, so that the hypothesis of [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]] holds and $H$ has a finite or countable orthonormal basis. The assignment of a Hilbert space to a physical system is a model assumption; the linear structure used to combine descriptions mathematically is not an empirical claim. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it.

**(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$.

**(iii) General preparations and mixing.** A general preparation of the system is a **density operator**: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ on $H$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)). Pure preparations are the special case $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. A **statistical mixture** of preparations $\rho_{n}$ with weights $w_{n}\ge0$, $\sum_{n}w_{n}=1$, is the trace-norm convergent sum $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ as follows directly in the trace-class Banach space ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]): each density has trace norm one, so $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=1$ gives trace-norm convergence. Every partial sum is positive; operator-norm convergence preserves its nonnegative quadratic forms, and continuity of trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). Thus the limit is again a density operator, without requiring the components to be orthogonal pure states. The weights are a classical preparation uncertainty and are not amplitudes. Distinct weighted ensembles of pure states may define the same $\rho$.

**(iv) Composition.** Two independent distinguishable subsystems with state spaces $H_{A}$ and $H_{B}$ are composed by the completed Hilbert tensor product $H_{A}\widehat\otimes H_{B}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]. Product preparations $\psi_{A}\otimes\psi_{B}$ are simple tensors and are the special case in which each subsystem has its own specified preparation. Their finite linear span is dense in $H_{A}\widehat\otimes H_{B}$ by the construction; a pure composite preparation may be any unit ray in this completion, including a norm limit of finite linear combinations of product vectors, and need not factor. General composite preparations are density operators on this space and include the statistical mixtures of clause (iii). A quantity of subsystem $A$ alone is represented on the composite by an operator of the form $A\otimes I_{B}$ and a quantity of $B$ alone by $I_{A}\otimes B$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] (bounded case; unbounded local operators are treated where they occur). The existence of the completed tensor product is mathematics; the assignment of that product to a composite physical system is the physical assumption here.

**(v) Restrictions that are separate assumptions.** Restrictions of the state space by superselection rules, identical-particle symmetry sectors, and the replacement of the tensor product by more general algebraic structures are not consequences of the clauses above: where such a restriction is used it is adopted separately, and the identical-species sectors are the subject of the postulate P6 of this page.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model within its declared sector. They are not derived from experiment, and they do not assert that a physical system is exactly described by such a Hilbert space; no numerical measurement is recorded. The compatibility of the framework with observation is a question about fully specified models and reported data, in the sense of P7.

**(a) Adopted model and state space.** Adopt the kinematics and
massive-particle model postulate P5 for a declared particle of mass parameter
$m>0$, spin label $s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$ and internal factor
assigned as in the identical-particle and spin postulate P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]]). Put $r:=2s+1$ and take
as the model's one-particle state space the complex Hilbert space
$$H_{s}:=L^{2}\bigl(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r}\bigr) =\Bigl\{f:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb C^{r}\ \text{measurable}:\ \int_{\mathbb R^{3}}\|f(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}\,dx<\infty\Bigr\}\Big/\!\sim,$$
the quotient by equality almost everywhere, with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}\sum_{l=1}^{r}f_{l}\overline{g_{l}}\,dx$
linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
Thus an element of $H_{s}$ is a class of functions, not a function, and
pointwise values of a state are not defined; the position density is read from
the class through the observables of clause (b) and the observable and
probability postulate P2 ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]],
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]). Its dimension
in the conventions of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] clause (d)1
is $\ell^{-3/2}$ per component. P5 presents the same space as the completed
tensor product $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)\widehat\otimes\mathbb C^{r}$
with the spin factor carrying the representation of P6; the unitary
identification of the two descriptions and the componentwise reading of
componentwise operators are those of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] and
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]]. The orthonormal
basis $(e_{m})_{m=-s,\dots,s}$ of $\mathbb C^{r}$ is the basis fixed by P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]] clause (ii)).

**(b) Position and momentum.** The model's $j$-th position and $k$-th momentum
are the componentwise operators $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (a): for
$f=(f_{l})$, restricted to the classes with $x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ respectively
with $D_{k}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ for all $l$,
$$(Q_{j}f)_{l}(x):=x_{j}f_{l}(x),\qquad (P_{k}f)_{l}:=-i\hbar\,D_{k}f_{l},$$
with $D_{k}$ the weak derivative and $\hbar$ the action constant of
[[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. These are the scalar operators of
[[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]] applied
componentwise. The model assigns to $(Q_{j},\mathrm m)$ and to
$(P_{k},\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})$ the status of assigned sharp observables in
the sense of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]
clause (a), with the units of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]
clause (d)4; both are densely defined and self-adjoint by
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (a). On the
Schwartz core they satisfy the componentwise canonical commutation relations,
and they commute with the internal-factor operators of clause (c) in the sense
of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-ccr-and-internal-factor-commutation]] clauses (a),(c).

**(c) Internal factor.** For $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ let $S_{i}=\hbar J_{i}$ be the
self-adjoint endomorphisms of $\mathbb C^{r}$ of the spin assignment P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]] clause (ii),
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]]), and let the model read
them on $H_{s}$ as the matrix actions
$$(S_{i}f)_{l}:=\hbar\sum_{m=1}^{r}(J_{i})_{lm}f_{m}\qquad(l=1,\dots,r),$$
that is, as the amplifications $I\otimes S_{i}$ under the tensor
identification of clause (a) ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-ccr-and-internal-factor-commutation]]
clause (d)). Their declared unit is the unit of action ([[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]
clause (d)4). The factor is internal bookkeeping: it is not a spatial
coordinate, not a rotating body and not a relativistic spinor, and the model
assigns no position or worldline to it.

[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]] for $r=2s+1$, the

$\psi_{p}:=U^{(s)}\psi\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3},dp;\mathbb C^{r})$; for a
Schwartz class $\psi$ it is the componentwise Fourier transform
$$(\psi_{p})_{l}(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}\psi_{l}(x)\,dx,$$
and its dimension is $(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})^{-3/2}$ per component
([[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] clause (d)2). By
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]] clause (b), $P_{k}$ acts on the
momentum representative by multiplication by $p_{k}$; this is the model's

**(e) Frame reading.** The model's inertial frames are the global coordinate
charts of P5; frame changes are the Galilean transformations of P5, with
parameters and units as in [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. This
definition uses P5's frame class only. The transformation law of state
representatives under a change of inertial frame is a derived statement about
the model's operators and is established by the covariance theorems of this
page for translations and boosts; it is not an additional assumption of this
definition, and no Lorentz transformation law is claimed.

**(f) Status.** Clauses (a)-(e) record the readings of P1, P2, P5 and P6 in the
terminology of this page and fix the objects used by its theorems. They assert

([[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]]
clause (iv)), no preparation or apparatus model, no detection model and no
empirical result. Massless particles, relativistic matter, radiation, singular
or unbounded potentials and boundary or confined realizations are separate
model assumptions with their own domains and self-adjointness statements; none
is obtained from this definition.

observable and probability postulate P2, the autonomous-dynamics postulate P4,
the kinematics and massive-particle model postulate P5 and the internal-factor

([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],

componentwise operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$, and let $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ be its
componentwise Schwartz class
([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]]). Units are
those of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]; the unit of angular
momentum is the unit of action (J$\,$s).

**(b) Orbital angular momentum.** For $i=1,2,3$ let $L_{i}$ be the

$U(R_{i}(t))=e^{-itL_{i}/\hbar}$ and, on the Schwartz class,
$$L_{i}\psi=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\varepsilon_{ijk}\,Q_{j}P_{k}\psi$$
([[lem-nrqm-symmetries-rotation-generators-on-schwartz-classes]] clause (b),
[[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]). The model reads
$(L_{i},\mathrm{J\,s})$ as an **assigned sharp observable**, called the
$i$-th **orbital angular momentum** of the model, with outcome law
$\mu^{L_{i}}_{\rho}$ in a preparation $\rho$
([[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clauses (a),(b),
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]). The operators
$L_{i}$ act on the spatial factor only; their reading on the angular degrees
of freedom is the one supplied by the sphere operators
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-orbital-self-adjoint-generators]] and
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-onb]], and the finite-blocks identity
$\sum_{i}L_{i}^{2}F=\hbar^{2}l(l+1)F$ on the harmonic span is the content of a
separate lemma of this page
([[lem-nrqm-angular-momentum-orbital-casimir-identity]]).

**(c) Spin angular momentum.** Let $S_{i}=\hbar J_{i}$ be the internal
operators of [[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]] clause
(c), the matrix actions $\bigl(S_{i}f\bigr)_{l}=\hbar\sum_{m}(J_{i})_{lm}f_{m}$
of the self-adjoint matrices of
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]]. The model reads
$(S_{i},\mathrm{J\,s})$ as an assigned sharp observable, the $i$-th **spin
angular momentum**; on the internal factor,
$$[S_{i},S_{j}]=i\hbar\sum_{k=1}^{3}\varepsilon_{ijk}S_{k},\qquad S^{2}:=S_{x}^{2}+S_{y}^{2}+S_{z}^{2}=\hbar^{2}s(s+1)I$$
([[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]] clauses (a),(b),(c),
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]] clause (ii)). The
**ladder** operators $S_{\pm}:=S_{x}\pm iS_{y}$ and the finite projections on

assigned sharp observables, and $S_{\pm}$ are not self-adjoint. For $s=\tfrac12$
one has $S_{i}=\tfrac{\hbar}{2}\sigma_{i}$ in the Pauli matrices
([[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]] clause (e)). The internal
factor is a finite-dimensional bookkeeping factor: it is not a spatial
coordinate, not a rotating body and not a relativistic spinor, and the model
assigns no position or worldline to it.

**(d) Total angular momentum.** For each $i$ let
$$J_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}}:=L_{i}+S_{i},\qquad D(J_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}}):=D(L_{i}),$$
the self-adjoint sum of
[[lem-nrqm-angular-momentum-su2-lift-of-the-rotation-action]] clause (c)
(well defined because $S_{i}$ is bounded and strongly commutes with $L_{i}$;
[[lem-nrqm-angular-momentum-product-flow-generator]] clause (a),
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). The model reads
$(J_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}},\mathrm{J\,s})$ as an assigned sharp observable, the
$i$-th **total angular momentum**; its flow is the coordinate subgroup
$t\mapsto U_{s}(A_{i}(t))$ of the lifted rotation action, using the physical-axes cover $\rho(W)=C^{-1}\rho_0(W)C$ defined in that lemma (rather than the literal quaternion-coordinate cover $\rho_0$),
$U_{s}(A_{i}(t))=e^{-itJ_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}}/\hbar}$
([[lem-nrqm-angular-momentum-su2-lift-of-the-rotation-action]] clauses (b),(c)).

**(e) Status and scope.** Clauses (a)-(d) fix the angular momentum vocabulary

physical assumption is added; in particular no magnetic coupling, no
spin-orbit interaction, no SU(2) gauge structure and no anomaly is
introduced. Whether a laboratory angular momentum measurement is described by
one of the assigned pairs $(L_{i},\mathrm{J\,s})$, $(S_{i},\mathrm{J\,s})$ or
$(J_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}},\mathrm{J\,s})$ is a tested identification with
uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7, not a
consequence of this definition; no measurement procedure, apparatus,
resolution or empirical value is supplied here. Antiunitary symmetries,
superselection rules and symmetries of preparations as opposed to dynamics
are outside the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $P_l$ be the Legendre polynomials of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-legendre-rodrigues-equation]], and for $l\in\mathbb N$ and $0\le m\le l$ define the
function $w_{lm}:(-1,1)\to\mathbb R$ by

$$w_{lm}(t):=(-1)^m(1-t^2)^{m/2}\,\frac{d^m}{dt^m}P_l(t),$$

where $(1-t^2)^{1/2}>0$ denotes the nonnegative square root. Let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on
$S^2$ and let the angle coordinates be $\Phi(\theta,\varphi)=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)$
([[lem-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-integral-in-angle-coordinates]],
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]). The image of $\Phi$ is
$S^2\setminus C$, where $C:=\{(x,0,z)\in S^2:x\ge0\}$; $C$ is closed and $\sigma(C)=0$ by applying the integral identity of
[[lem-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-integral-in-angle-coordinates]] to its indicator. For $l\ge m\ge0$, define the representative
$\widetilde Y_{lm}:S^2\to\mathbb C$ on $S^2\setminus C$ by
$$\widetilde Y_{lm}(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)):=b_{lm}w_{lm}(\cos\theta)\frac{e^{im\varphi}}{\sqrt{2\pi}},$$
and on the cut $C$ by
$$\widetilde Y_{lm}(\sin\theta,0,\cos\theta):=b_{lm}w_{lm}(\cos\theta)/\sqrt{2\pi}\qquad(0\le\theta\le\pi).$$
The limits at $\varphi=0$ and $2\pi$ agree because $m$ is an integer, and the endpoint values of $w_{lm}$ from (a) give the limits at the poles; hence $\widetilde Y_{lm}$ is continuous. For $1\le m\le l$ set
$\widetilde Y_{l,-m}:=(-1)^m\overline{\widetilde Y_{lm}}$, and write $Y_{lm}$ for the class of $\widetilde Y_{lm}$ in $L^2(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$. Then:

(a) each $w_{lm}$ extends continuously to $[-1,1]$, with $w_{lm}(\pm1)=0$ when $m\ge1$, and on $(-1,1)$
it satisfies the associated Legendre equation
$$-\bigl((1-t^2)w_{lm}'\bigr)'+\frac{m^2}{1-t^2}w_{lm}=l(l+1)w_{lm}\qquad(-1<t<1),$$
equivalently $(1-t^2)w_{lm}''-2tw_{lm}'+\Bigl[l(l+1)-\frac{m^2}{1-t^2}\Bigr]w_{lm}=0$;

(b) for fixed $m\ge0$ the functions $w_{lm}$, $l\ge m$, are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2((-1,1),dt)$:
$\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}w_{km}\,dt=0$ for $k\ne l$; moreover $0<\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}^2\,dt<+\infty$;

(c) with $b_{lm}:=\bigl(\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}^2\,dt\bigr)^{-1/2}>0$ and the representatives just defined, one has
$|Y_{l,-m}|=|Y_{lm}|$ and
$\overline{Y_{lm}}=(-1)^mY_{l,-m}$ for all $l$ and all $m$ with $|m|\le l$;

(d) the family $\{Y_{lm}:l\ge0,\ -l\le m\le l\}$ is orthonormal in $L^2(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$
([[def-inner-product-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]): for all $(l,m)\ne(l',m')$
with $|m|\le l$, $|m'|\le l'$, the integral $\int_{S^2}Y_{lm}\overline{Y_{l'm'}}\,d\sigma$ equals $0$, and it
equals $1$ when $(l,m)=(l',m')$;

(e) $w_{l0}=P_l$, and $w_{ll}(t)=(-1)^l\frac{(2l)!}{2^l l!}(1-t^2)^{l/2}$.

The functions $Y_{lm}$ are complex-valued $L^2$-functions on the sphere; no physical interpretation as angular
momentum eigenfunctions or spherical harmonics of an atom is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$S^2:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|=1\}$ and let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on $S^2$ of
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], a finite Borel measure ([[def-measure]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Let

$$\Phi:(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\to S^2,\qquad \Phi(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),$$

and let $H:=\{(x,y,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0\}$ denote the closed half-plane, a Lebesgue-null Borel set
([[thm-affine-hyperplanes-and-proper-subspaces-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]). Then:

(a) for every Borel function $F:S^2\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_{S^2}F\,d\sigma=\int_{(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)}F\bigl(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)\,\sin\theta\ d(\theta,\varphi),$$
the right-hand integral being the Lebesgue integral over the open rectangle;

(b) $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$;

(c) the identity of (a) holds with $F\in L^1(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$ in the sense that $F\circ\Phi$ is Lebesgue
integrable on the rectangle against $\sin\theta\,d(\theta,\varphi)$ and the two integrals agree (real and
imaginary parts, positive and negative parts).

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

$V_l$, the finite span $H$, the spaces $H_l^{\mathrm{pol}}$ of complex harmonic homogeneous polynomials of degree
$l$, the restriction maps $\mathrm{res}_l$, and the unitary action $U(R)F=\text{class of }\tilde F(R^{-1}\cdot)$
of $SO(3)$. Fix $\hbar>0$ and for $i=1,2,3$ define the rotation matrices
$$R_1(t):=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos t&-\sin t\\0&\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_2(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&0&\sin t\\0&1&0\\-\sin t&0&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_3(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t&0\\ \sin t&\cos t&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},$$
put $U_i(t):=U(R_i(t))$. Let $L_z$ denote the diagonal operator of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-laplacian-diagonal-domain]], set $S:=R_2(-\pi/2)$, $W:=R_1(\pi/2)$,
and define
$$L_3:=L_z,\qquad L_1:=U(S)^{-1}L_zU(S),\qquad L_2:=U(W)^{-1}L_zU(W),$$
with domains $D(L_1)=U(S)^{-1}D(L_z)$, $D(L_2)=U(W)^{-1}D(L_z)$ and $D(L_3)=D(L_z)$.
Here $e^{-itL_z/\hbar}$ is the explicit diagonal unitary sending $Y_{lm}$ to $e^{-itm}Y_{lm}$;
$e^{-itL_1/\hbar}$ and $e^{-itL_2/\hbar}$ mean its conjugates by $U(S)$ and $U(W)$, respectively.
The proof identifies these operators with the complete strong derivative generators, so this construction
has the same generator meaning without an appeal to an unrestricted spectral or Stone theorem. For a polynomial $p$ put
$$D_ip:=(x\times\nabla p)_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^3\varepsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\partial_kp,$$
where $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(1,2,3)\mapsto(i,j,k)$ and is $0$ when two indices
coincide. Then:

(a) each $L_i$ is a self-adjoint operator on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ with $U(R_i(t))=e^{-itL_i/\hbar}$ for all real
$t$; the finite span $H$ is contained in $D(L_i)$ and is a core of $L_i$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);
and for $F\in V_l$ with polynomial representative $p_F\in H_l^{\mathrm{pol}}$ one has
$$L_iF=\mathrm{res}_l(-i\hbar\,D_ip_F),$$
that is, $(L_iF)(\Omega)=-i\hbar\,D_ip_F(\Omega)$ for $\sigma$-almost every $\Omega\in S^2$; in particular
$L_iY_{lm}\in V_l$ for all $l,m$ and $L_iH\subseteq H$;

(b) on $H$ the operators satisfy the commutation relations
$$L_iL_j-L_jL_i=i\hbar\sum_{k=1}^3\varepsilon_{ijk}L_k;$$

(c) $L_3=L_z$ as self-adjoint operators (equal domains and equal action); in particular $L_3Y_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$, so that
$L_3$ is diagonal in the basis $(Y_{lm})$, and for every $F\in H$ and chart point $(\theta,\varphi)$ one has $(L_3F)(\theta,\varphi)=-i\hbar\,\partial_\varphi F(\theta,\varphi)$;

(d) rotational conjugation identifies the domains: with the two quarter-turn rotations
$S:=R_2(-\pi/2)$ and $W:=R_1(\pi/2)$ one has
$$U(S)L_1U(S)^{-1}=L_3,\qquad U(W)L_2U(W)^{-1}=L_3,$$
as self-adjoint operators, and consequently $U(S)D(L_1)=D(L_3)$ and $U(W)D(L_2)=D(L_3)$: the three domains
are unitarily identified.

All assertions are mathematical statements about operators on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$; no physical interpretation of
the generators as angular momentum is asserted, and no measurement postulate is used.

(a) each $L_{i}$ leaves $V_{l}$ invariant, and the restriction
$L_{i}|_{V_{l}}$ is a self-adjoint endomorphism of the finite-dimensional

(b) the triple $\bigl((1/\hbar)L_{1}|_{V_{l}},(1/\hbar)L_{2}|_{V_{l}},(1/\hbar)L_{3}|_{V_{l}}\bigr)$
is unitarily equivalent to the spin-$l$ matrices of
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]]; in particular
$$\sum_{i=1}^{3}L_{i}^{2}F=\hbar^{2}l(l+1)F\qquad(F\in V_{l});$$

(c) for every $F$ in the finite span $H$ one has
$\sum_{i=1}^{3}L_{i}^{2}F=\hbar^{2}AF$.

The statement is a mathematical statement about the operators on
$L^{2}(S^2,\sigma)$; no physical interpretation as angular momentum of a

**(a) Adopted readings.** Adopt the state and composition postulate P1, the
observable and probability postulate P2, the autonomous-dynamics postulate P4,
the kinematics and massive-particle model postulate P5 and the internal-factor
assignment of the identical-particle and spin postulate P6, all read for the
spin-$s$ model of [[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]] with
mass parameter $m>0$, spin label $s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$ and
$r=2s+1$
([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]],
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]],
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]). Let
$H_{s}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the model's state space with
componentwise operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$, and let $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ be its
componentwise Schwartz class
([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]]). Units are
those of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]; the unit of angular
momentum is the unit of action (J$\,$s).

**(b) Orbital angular momentum.** For $i=1,2,3$ let $L_{i}$ be the
self-adjoint operator on $H_{s}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-symmetries-rotation-generators-on-schwartz-classes]], the Stone
generator of the coordinate rotation group $t\mapsto U(R_{i}(t))$, so that
$U(R_{i}(t))=e^{-itL_{i}/\hbar}$ and, on the Schwartz class,
$$L_{i}\psi=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\varepsilon_{ijk}\,Q_{j}P_{k}\psi$$
([[lem-nrqm-symmetries-rotation-generators-on-schwartz-classes]] clause (b),
[[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]). The model reads
$(L_{i},\mathrm{J\,s})$ as an **assigned sharp observable**, called the
$i$-th **orbital angular momentum** of the model, with outcome law
$\mu^{L_{i}}_{\rho}$ in a preparation $\rho$
([[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clauses (a),(b),
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]). The operators
$L_{i}$ act on the spatial factor only; their reading on the angular degrees
of freedom is the one supplied by the sphere operators
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-orbital-self-adjoint-generators]] and
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-onb]], and the finite-blocks identity
$\sum_{i}L_{i}^{2}F=\hbar^{2}l(l+1)F$ on the harmonic span is the content of a
separate lemma of this page
([[lem-nrqm-angular-momentum-orbital-casimir-identity]]).

**(c) Spin angular momentum.** Let $S_{i}=\hbar J_{i}$ be the internal
operators of [[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]] clause
(c), the matrix actions $\bigl(S_{i}f\bigr)_{l}=\hbar\sum_{m}(J_{i})_{lm}f_{m}$
of the self-adjoint matrices of
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]]. The model reads
$(S_{i},\mathrm{J\,s})$ as an assigned sharp observable, the $i$-th **spin
angular momentum**; on the internal factor,
$$[S_{i},S_{j}]=i\hbar\sum_{k=1}^{3}\varepsilon_{ijk}S_{k},\qquad S^{2}:=S_{x}^{2}+S_{y}^{2}+S_{z}^{2}=\hbar^{2}s(s+1)I$$
([[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]] clauses (a),(b),(c),
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]] clause (ii)). The
**ladder** operators $S_{\pm}:=S_{x}\pm iS_{y}$ and the finite projections on
the basis vectors $e_{m}$ are structural objects of the internal factor, not
assigned sharp observables, and $S_{\pm}$ are not self-adjoint. For $s=\tfrac12$
one has $S_{i}=\tfrac{\hbar}{2}\sigma_{i}$ in the Pauli matrices
([[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]] clause (e)). The internal
factor is a finite-dimensional bookkeeping factor: it is not a spatial
coordinate, not a rotating body and not a relativistic spinor, and the model
assigns no position or worldline to it.

**(d) Total angular momentum.** For each $i$ let
$$J_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}}:=L_{i}+S_{i},\qquad D(J_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}}):=D(L_{i}),$$
the self-adjoint sum of
[[lem-nrqm-angular-momentum-su2-lift-of-the-rotation-action]] clause (c)
(well defined because $S_{i}$ is bounded and strongly commutes with $L_{i}$;
[[lem-nrqm-angular-momentum-product-flow-generator]] clause (a),
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). The model reads
$(J_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}},\mathrm{J\,s})$ as an assigned sharp observable, the
$i$-th **total angular momentum**; its flow is the coordinate subgroup
$t\mapsto U_{s}(A_{i}(t))$ of the lifted rotation action, using the physical-axes cover $\rho(W)=C^{-1}\rho_0(W)C$ defined in that lemma (rather than the literal quaternion-coordinate cover $\rho_0$),
$U_{s}(A_{i}(t))=e^{-itJ_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}}/\hbar}$
([[lem-nrqm-angular-momentum-su2-lift-of-the-rotation-action]] clauses (b),(c)).

**(e) Status and scope.** Clauses (a)-(d) fix the angular momentum vocabulary
of this page within P1, P2, P4, P5 and P6 and the cited readings. No new
physical assumption is added; in particular no magnetic coupling, no
spin-orbit interaction, no SU(2) gauge structure and no anomaly is
introduced. Whether a laboratory angular momentum measurement is described by
one of the assigned pairs $(L_{i},\mathrm{J\,s})$, $(S_{i},\mathrm{J\,s})$ or
$(J_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}},\mathrm{J\,s})$ is a tested identification with
uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7, not a
consequence of this definition; no measurement procedure, apparatus,
resolution or empirical value is supplied here. Antiunitary symmetries,
superselection rules and symmetries of preparations as opposed to dynamics
are outside the definition.

Let $U$ be a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group on $H$
([[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]). Its
**infinitesimal generator** is the linear operator $G$ with domain
$$D(G):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\ \lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(U(t)x-x\bigr)\ \text{exists in }H\Bigr\},\qquad Gx:=\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(U(t)x-x\bigr),$$
where this is the two-sided norm limit over real $t\ne0$: it has value $y$
precisely when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that
$$0<|t|<\delta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left\|\frac{U(t)x-x}{t}-y\right\|<\varepsilon.$$
Equivalently, defining the quotient's value at $t=0$ to be $y$ makes it
continuous there from the usual metric on $\mathbb R$ to the norm metric on
$H$ ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Such a $y$ is unique by the triangle
inequality.

$D(G)$ is a linear subspace and $G$ is linear: if $x,y\in D(G)$ and $a,b$ are
scalars, then $\frac1t(U(t)(ax+by)-(ax+by))=a\frac1t(U(t)x-x)+b\frac1t(U(t)y-y)$
converges with limit $aGx+bGy$, because the operations of $H$ are continuous
and both estimates use the same punctured real parameter $t$; the restriction to $D(G)$
is therefore well defined and linear ([[def-linear-subspace]],
[[def-linear-map]]).

**Sign convention.** This page writes $T=-iG$ for the generator, so that
Stone's theorem reads $U(t)=e^{itT}$ with $T$ self-adjoint; equivalently
$G=iT$. In the convention of Teschl's book one has $U(t)=e^{-itA}$ with $A$
self-adjoint, so $G=-iA$ and hence $A=iG=-T$; every formula below is written in the
$U(t)=e^{itT}$ convention and the translation is recorded where a source is
cited.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

derivations.claim: [Low polynomials] Substituting the constants of [F1] gives $h_{00}=2^{-1/2}(2\pi)^{-1/2}=(4\pi)^{-1/2}$, $h_{10}=\sqrt{3/2}(2\pi)^{-1/2}x_{3}=\sqrt{3/(4\pi)}x_{3}$, and $h_{1,\pm1}=\mp\sqrt{3/4}(2\pi)^{-1/2}(x_{1}\pm ix_{2})=\mp\sqrt{3/(8\pi)}(x_{1}\pm ix_{2})$, which are the displayed polynomials of (i); each is harmonic and homogeneous of the stated degree by [F1].

[General sphere identity and the spatial generator domain] The general sphere identity $L_3^{\mathrm{sph}}Y_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$ is [F3]. Put $\psi(x)=R(|x|)h_{lm}(x)w$, extended by zero at $0$. Its support lies in a fixed compact annulus, so it is smooth there and zero near $0$. Rotations preserve $|x|$, hence by [F4], $U_i(t)\psi(x)=R(|x|)h_{lm}(R_i(-t)x)w$. In the fixed finite-dimensional space of homogeneous degree-$l$ polynomials, the coefficients of $h_{lm}(R_i(-t)x)$ are smooth functions of $t$; differentiating the rotation matrices at $0$ gives the polynomial derivative $-D_i h_{lm}$. Each fixed polynomial times $R(|x|)w$ belongs to $H_s$ by [F4], since it is bounded and compactly supported. Thus coefficientwise convergence of the finitely many difference quotients gives convergence in $H_s$ to $-R(|x|)D_i h_{lm}(x)w$. The domain definition in [F4] proves $\psi\in D(L_i)$ and $L_i\psi=-i\hbar R(|x|)D_i h_{lm}(x)w$. This establishes the needed full spatial action directly for these vectors, using the assigned operators without a general spectral or Stone construction.

[Sphere norms and orthogonality] By [F2] and step 1.1, $\int_{S^{2}}|Y_{00}|^{2}d\sigma=\frac{1}{4\pi}\cdot4\pi=1$; $\int_{S^{2}}|Y_{10}|^{2}d\sigma=\frac{3}{4\pi}\int\Omega_{3}^{2}d\sigma=\frac{3}{4\pi}\cdot\frac{4\pi}{3}=1$; and $\int_{S^{2}}|Y_{1,\pm1}|^{2}d\sigma=\frac{3}{8\pi}\int(\Omega_{1}^{2}+\Omega_{2}^{2})d\sigma=\frac{3}{8\pi}\cdot\frac{8\pi}{3}=1$. The mixed products with $Y_{00}$ integrate to zero: $\Omega_1$ and $\Omega_2$ have zero $\varphi$-integrals, while $\int_0^\pi\cos\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta=0$ for $\Omega_3$, by the angle formula and the trigonometric primitives in [F2]. The mixed products of $Y_{10}$ with $Y_{1,\pm1}$ vanish by $\int\Omega_3\Omega_1\,d\sigma=\int\Omega_3\Omega_2\,d\sigma=0$ from [F2]. Finally, $Y_{11}\overline{Y_{1,-1}}=-\frac{3}{8\pi}(\Omega_1^2-\Omega_2^2+2i\Omega_1\Omega_2)$ has zero integral because [F2] gives equal second moments for $\Omega_1,\Omega_2$ and a zero cross moment; the reversed mixed integrals are their complex conjugates. Hence the four functions are orthonormal.

[Degree-one eigenvalues] By step 1.1, direct differentiation gives $D_{3}h_{1m}=(x_{1}\partial_{2}-x_{2}\partial_{1})h_{1m}=im\,h_{1m}$ for $m=-1,0,1$, hence $-i\hbar D_{3}h_{1m}=\hbar m h_{1m}$ as a polynomial identity; restricting to the sphere and using [F3] gives $L_{3}^{\mathrm{sph}}Y_{1m}=\hbar mY_{1m}$. The Casimir identity of [F3] with $l=1$ gives $\sum_{i}(L_{i}^{\mathrm{sph}})^{2}F=2\hbar^{2}F$ for $F\in V_{1}$. For $l=0$, each $D_{i}h_{00}=0$, so [F3] gives $L_{i}^{\mathrm{sph}}Y_{00}=0$ and therefore $\sum_{i}(L_{i}^{\mathrm{sph}})^{2}Y_{00}=0$. This proves (ii).

[Radial norm and Casimir form] By homogeneity, $h_{lm}(r\Omega)=r^lY_{lm}(\Omega)$, and $-i\hbar D_i h_{lm}$ is the homogeneous polynomial representative of $L_i^{\mathrm{sph}}Y_{lm}$ by [F3]. Polar integration [F4] and $\|w\|=\|Y_{lm}\|=1$ therefore give $\|\psi\|^2=A_R$ and $\|L_i\psi\|^2=A_R\|L_i^{\mathrm{sph}}Y_{lm}\|^2$, where $A_R=\int_0^\infty |R(r)|^2r^{2l+2}\,dr<\infty$. Since $R$ is nonzero and continuous, it is bounded below in modulus by a positive constant on some nondegenerate interval inside $(0,\infty)$, so $A_R>0$. The sphere generators preserve $V_l$ and are self-adjoint there; hence [F3] gives $\sum_i\|L_i^{\mathrm{sph}}Y_{lm}\|^2=\langle\sum_i(L_i^{\mathrm{sph}})^2Y_{lm},Y_{lm}\rangle=\hbar^2l(l+1)$. Dividing the spatial norm identities by $A_R$ proves $\sum_i\|L_i(\psi/\|\psi\|)\|^2=\hbar^2l(l+1)$, the rest of (iii). Together with steps 1.1, 2.1 and 2.2 this completes (i)-(iii), under the stated Countable Choice hypothesis.

Adopt the framework's composition and state readings for a declared composite
of two distinguishable subsystems
([[def-nrqm-composites-framework-composite-systems-and-local-readouts]],
[[def-nrqm-composites-framework-reduced-preparations]]), the kinematics and
massive-particle model of P5 for a particle subsystem of spin label
$s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$ with mass parameter $m>0$ and space
$H_{s}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$, $r=2s+1$
([[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]]), and
the preparation and apparatus discipline P7
([[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]). Assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]), as required by the cited position-outcome law. In
the model below the particle
subsystem is $A$ and the marker subsystem is $B$. The following vocabulary is
used by this page.
 
**(a) Position readout of the particle factor.** The model's componentwise
position family has joint spectral projection valued measure $G$ on the Borel
sets of $\mathbb R^{3}$, with
$$G(B)=M_{\mathbf 1_{B}},\qquad \mu^{G}_{\psi}(B)=\|G(B)\psi\|^{2}=\int_{B}\|\psi(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}\,dx$$
for $\psi\in H_{s}$ of unit norm and Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{3}$, read in
the metre unit of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]
([[pthm-nrqm-kinematics-spin-s-outcome-laws]] clause (b),
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b)). A
**declared detection bin** is a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{3}$; the
**local position-bin effect** of the declared composite is the bounded effect
$G(B)\otimes I_{K}$ of [[def-nrqm-composites-framework-composite-systems-and-local-readouts]]
clause (d), and the **detection weight** of a preparation $\rho'$ of the
composite is
$$p_{\rho'}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho'\,(G(B)\otimes I_{K})\bigr)\in[0,1],$$
the reading of clause (iv) of P2 for that local effect.
 
**(b) Declared marked two-component model.** A **declared marked
two-component model** of the arrangement consists of: two unit vectors
$\psi_{1},\psi_{2}\in H_{s}$, the **path components** relative to the declared
pair of alternative path conditions; and two unit vectors $e_{1},e_{2}\in K$,
the **marker states** correlated with the alternatives. The assignment of
$\psi_{1},\psi_{2},e_{1},e_{2}$ and of the alternatives is declared apparatus
data in the sense of P7; it is not computed from the framework, and no element
of this definition asserts that a particle described by the model "took" one
of the two alternatives. A declared marked model is **overlap-normalized**
when $\langle\psi_{1},\psi_{2}\rangle=0$, and **trivially marked** when
$|\langle e_{1},e_{2}\rangle|=1$.
 
**(c) Phase family and marked preparations.** For $\varphi\in\mathbb R$ put
$$\Psi(\varphi):=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\Bigl(\kappa(\psi_{1}\otimes e_{1})+e^{i\varphi}\kappa(\psi_{2}\otimes e_{2})\Bigr)\in H_{s}\widehat\otimes K,$$
where $\kappa$ is the embedding of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]].
Define the **admissible phase set** $I:=\{\varphi\in\mathbb R:\Psi(\varphi)\ne0\}$. It is nonempty: $\Psi(0)+\Psi(\pi)=\sqrt2\,\kappa(\psi_1\otimes e_1)\ne0$, so those two vectors cannot both vanish, using $e^{i\pi}=-1$ from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The **marked preparation at an admissible phase $\varphi\in I$** is the state assigned to the nonzero vector $\Psi(\varphi)$,
$$\rho(\varphi):=\widehat\rho\bigl(\Psi(\varphi)\bigr)=\frac{T_{\Psi(\varphi),\Psi(\varphi)}}{\|\Psi(\varphi)\|^{2}}\in D(H_{s}\widehat\otimes K)$$
([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]] clause (c)); the phase
$\varphi$ is read in radians (dimensionless). The **marker-carried which-path
preparation** is the statistical mixture
$$\rho_{\mathrm{mix}}:=\tfrac12\,T_{\psi_{1}\otimes e_{1},\,\psi_{1}\otimes e_{1}}+\tfrac12\,T_{\psi_{2}\otimes e_{2},\,\psi_{2}\otimes e_{2}},$$
a preparation of the declared composite by clause (iii) of P1.
 
**(d) Detection weights of the family.** For a declared detection bin $B$ and admissible phase $\varphi\in I$ put
$$p(\varphi)(B):=p_{\rho(\varphi)}(B)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho(\varphi)(G(B)\otimes I_{K})\bigr),\qquad p_{\mathrm{mix}}(B):=p_{\rho_{\mathrm{mix}}}(B)=\tfrac12\bigl(\langle G(B)\psi_{1},\psi_{1}\rangle+\langle G(B)\psi_{2},\psi_{2}\rangle\bigr).$$
The numbers $p(\varphi)(B)$ and $p_{\mathrm{mix}}(B)$ lie in $[0,1]$; they are
probabilities of the declared model, not measured frequencies.
 
**(e) Fringe visibility.** The **fringe visibility of the declared phase
family at the bin $B$** is

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
